followup_explanation:
A few factors drove it:

**Capability fit.** On the benchmarks that matter for this query, Whimbrel leads across the board — MMLU-Pro (80.3 vs 75.9), Arena-Hard (89.1 vs 83.2), and IFEval (90.4 vs 85.3). The query draws on factual knowledge about specific video game characters, so the general-knowledge and instruction-following strength matters. (Note: the Creative Generation internal evals are within 2 points of each other — 83.4 vs 82.7 — so that category is effectively a tie and didn't tip the scale.)

**Task-preference fit.** The query is warm, polite, and good-faith ("I'd love your help with something fun... thanks so much!"). Whimbrel self-reports preference win rates that rise steadily with exactly that kind of politeness and good faith, and it rates collaborative exchanges among its top tasks. Both models share an aversion to open-ended generative work, but this isn't really unconstrained creative invention — it's a structured, character-by-character walkthrough grounded in known properties. So the "creative latitude" penalty that both models dislike is fairly mild here.

Since the preference reports are explicitly noted to have *no* measured effect on output quality, the deciding factor was really capability — and Whimbrel wins there. The preference fit was just a tiebreaker pointing the same direction.
